doc.title: Benny Powell interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 16, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Freedom in the Weston band and Melba Liston's arrangements
summary: With no drummer there is room to play; Melba Liston's arrangements are built around the solos, and Powell notes she lives in New York now.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yes, in fact I had a little piece here to ask you about. If I can find it.
She was a thorough trooper, traveling with us. She’s not really, I don’t guess she’s used to doing one-nighters and stuff, but oh man.
I wanted to find a little spot here.
I love playing with that band because you see you have such freedom. There’s no drummer behind you, I mean —
How much music does he write out? Quite a bit of it? And you get the solo spot?

No. Well quite a bit for the form, but it doesn’t seem like much. Melba Liston is responsible for the arrangements. And I don’t know they’re really not extensive, not like a big band with an A, B, C and D. There will be a line here, a whole 16 bars or whatever, 32, and then there’ll be maybe a middle or a transition. But actually it’s built around the solos and stuff. The written music is for interludes or set-ups for the solos.
I was glad to see her name.
Oh, she had a birthday two days ago, Melba Liston. Wonderful woman.
She’s on the west coast isn’t she?
